unit-testing.definition: Testing individual functions, classes, or modules in isolation from the rest of the system.

integration-testing.definition: Testing interactions and data flow between combined components, services, or modules.

system-testing.definition: Testing the fully integrated system end to end against its functional and non-functional requirements.

acceptance-testing.definition: Validating that the system satisfies business requirements and is fit for release.

user-acceptance-testing-uat.definition: Real users or business representatives validate the system in a production-like environment before sign-off.

functional-testing.definition: Verifying that features behave according to specified functional requirements.

non-functional-testing.definition: Verifying quality attributes such as performance, security, reliability, and usability rather than behaviour.

smoke-testing.definition: A shallow build-verification suite confirming critical paths work before deeper testing begins.

sanity-testing.definition: Narrow, focused testing after a small change to confirm a specific fix or area is stable.

regression-testing.definition: Re-testing existing behaviour to ensure new changes have not broken previously working functionality.

end-to-end-e2e-testing.definition: Exercising complete user journeys across the real stack, front end to back end and dependencies.

performance-testing.definition: Measuring responsiveness, throughput, and resource use under defined workloads.

load-testing.definition: Verifying behaviour at expected production load, including peak traffic levels.

stress-testing.definition: Pushing the system beyond normal capacity to find breaking points and failure behaviour.

endurance-testing.definition: Sustained load over long duration to expose memory leaks, degradation, and resource exhaustion.

spike-testing.definition: Sudden, extreme bursts of load to verify the system absorbs and recovers from traffic surges.

volume-testing.definition: Testing with large volumes of data to validate storage, processing, and query behaviour at scale.

scalability-testing.definition: Measuring how throughput and latency change as resources, nodes, or users are added.

security-testing.definition: Assessing a system for vulnerabilities, weaknesses, and compliance with security requirements.

penetration-testing.definition: Authorised simulated attacks that exploit weaknesses to prove real-world impact.

usability-testing.definition: Observing real users to assess effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction of the interface.

accessibility-testing.definition: Verifying conformance with accessibility standards so users with disabilities can operate the product.

compatibility-testing.definition: Verifying correct behaviour across browsers, devices, OS versions, and environments.

reliability-testing.definition: Measuring the probability of failure-free operation over time under stated conditions.

maintainability-testing.definition: Assessing how easily the system can be understood, modified, extended, and repaired.

localization-testing.definition: Validating translations, formats, imagery, and culture-specific behaviour for a target locale.

internationalization-testing.definition: Verifying the product is locale-neutral and can support new languages without code changes.

black-box-testing.definition: Deriving tests from external behaviour and specifications without knowledge of internals.

white-box-testing.definition: Designing tests from internal structure, code paths, and implementation knowledge.

grey-box-testing.definition: Testing that combines external interfaces with partial knowledge of internal structure.

manual-testing.definition: Human-executed testing relying on judgement, observation, and exploration.

automation-testing.definition: Executing tests via scripts and frameworks for speed, repeatability, and CI integration.

exploratory-testing.definition: Simultaneous learning, test design, and execution driven by tester judgement.

ad-hoc-testing.definition: Informal, unstructured testing without documentation or planning.

monkey-testing.definition: Random or semi-random inputs or actions to check the system does not crash catastrophically.

gorilla-testing.definition: Repeated deep testing of one high-risk functionality until confidence is achieved.

boundary-value-testing.definition: Testing at the edges of input domains where defects cluster: min, max, and just beyond.

equivalence-partitioning-testing.definition: Dividing inputs into classes that should behave identically and testing one representative per class.

mutation-testing.definition: Seeding small faults into code to measure whether the test suite detects them.

static-testing.definition: Examining code, documents, or models without executing them, as in reviews and static analysis.

dynamic-testing.definition: Executing the software to observe behaviour, outputs, and runtime properties.

alpha-testing.definition: Internal testing at the developer's site before external release.

beta-testing.definition: Real users test a near-final release in their own environment before general availability.

a-b-testing.definition: Randomised controlled comparison of two variants to measure causal impact on a metric.

recovery-testing.definition: Verifying the system recovers correctly from crashes, faults, and interrupted operations.

configuration-testing.definition: Testing behaviour across supported hardware, software, and configuration combinations.

installation-testing.definition: Verifying install, upgrade, migration, rollback, and uninstall paths across environments.

visual-testing.definition: Detecting unintended visual changes in UI rendering, layout, and pixels.

api-testing.definition: Validating endpoints, contracts, status codes, schemas, and integration behaviour directly.

database-testing.definition: Verifying schema, integrity constraints, transactions, stored logic, and data correctness.

resilience-engineering.definition: The discipline of designing socio-technical systems that can adapt and succeed under varying conditions.

site-reliability-engineering.definition: Applying software engineering to operations, run by engineers who own reliability with explicit objectives.

fault-tolerance.definition: A system's ability to keep operating correctly when components fail.

dynamic-analysis.definition: Analysing software by executing it, observing runtime behaviour, memory, and coverage.

vulnerability-scanning.definition: Automated discovery of known weaknesses in code, dependencies, containers, and hosts.

fuzz-testing.definition: Feeding malformed or random inputs at scale to find crashes, hangs, and safety violations.

chaos-mesh.definition: A Kubernetes-native chaos engineering platform injecting pod, network, IO, and time faults as CRDs.

disaster-recovery.definition: Restoring systems and data after catastrophic loss, with defined priorities and procedures.

failure-mode-and-effects-analysis.definition: Systematically enumerating how each component can fail and the consequences of each failure mode.

red-teaming.definition: Adversarial simulation targeting an organisation's people, processes, and technology end to end.

automated-rollback.definition: Reversing a bad deployment automatically on health or SLO regression.

circuit-breaking.definition: Stopping calls to a failing dependency to prevent cascading failure and allow recovery.

rate-limiting.definition: Constraining request volume per client or scope to protect capacity and fairness.

blast-radius-mitigation.definition: Limiting the scope of impact a single failure or bad change can cause.

infrastructure-as-code-testing.definition: Verifying IaC definitions with unit, policy, plan, and integration tests before applying them.

chaos-monkey.definition: Netflix's tool that randomly terminates production instances to enforce resilience by design.

game-days.definition: Scheduled, team-wide rehearsals of failure scenarios in production-like conditions.

post-mortem-analysis.definition: Structured review after an incident to establish causes and prevent recurrence.

software-rejuvenation.definition: Periodically restarting or refreshing software to clear accumulated state and latent failures.

proactive-monitoring.definition: Detecting degradation and predicting issues before users are affected.

observability.definition: The ability to understand internal system state from its external outputs of metrics, logs, and traces.

synthetic-monitoring.definition: Scripted probes testing user journeys from outside, independent of real traffic.

degradation-testing.definition: Verifying how a system behaves as resources or dependencies degrade, and that it fails gracefully.

infrastructure-hardening.definition: Reducing attack surface through baselines, minimal images, patching, and disabling unnecessary services.

test-driven-development-tdd.definition: Write a failing test first, make it pass with minimal code, then refactor: the red-green-refactor loop.

acceptance-test-driven-development-atdd.definition: Collaboratively define acceptance tests up front, then build to satisfy them.

behavior-driven-development-bdd.definition: Evolving behaviour through examples in shared business language; specs become executable tests.

continuous-testing.definition: Running automated tests throughout the delivery pipeline for rapid, continuous feedback.

canary-testing.definition: Exposing a small slice of real traffic to a new version and comparing health before full rollout.

capacity-testing.definition: Determining the maximum load the system can sustain while meeting its SLOs.

benchmarking.definition: Measuring and comparing system or component performance against a defined baseline or rivals.

conformance-testing.definition: Verifying an implementation meets a formal standard or protocol specification.

interoperability-testing.definition: Proving that independently built systems can exchange and correctly use information together.

risk-based-testing.definition: Prioritising test effort by likelihood and impact of failure to focus on what matters most.

test-environment-management.definition: Provisioning, versioning, isolating, and refreshing environments needed for reliable testing.

test-data-management.definition: Governed creation, masking, subsetting, and lifecycle of data used for testing.

synthetic-test-data.definition: Artificially generated data that mimics production characteristics without exposing real records.

production-traffic-replay-shadow-testing.definition: Mirroring real production requests to a candidate version and comparing behaviour offline.

record-and-replay-testing.definition: Capturing real interactions once, then deterministically replaying them as regression tests.

time-travel-testing.definition: Controlling or simulating system clock and time zones to test time-dependent behaviour deterministically.

bug-bash.definition: A time-boxed, team-wide hunt for defects in a build, often before release.

dogfooding.definition: Using your own product internally to surface defects and friction before customers do.

crowdtesting.definition: Outsourcing testing to a large distributed community across diverse real devices and locales.

pair-testing.definition: Two people test together, typically one driving and one observing and questioning.

regression-test-selection.definition: Automatically choosing the minimal subset of tests impacted by a code change.

test-prioritisation.definition: Ordering tests to maximise early detection of severe defects under time constraints.

test-suite-reduction.definition: Shrinking a test suite while preserving its defect-detection capability.

traceability-matrix.definition: A mapping grid linking requirements to tests, code, and defects for coverage and audit.

requirements-traceability.definition: Following each requirement through design, code, tests, and releases to prove coverage.

specification-by-example.definition: Deriving a shared, testable specification from concrete examples agreed with the business.

three-amigos.definition: Business, development, and testing roles reviewing a story together before coding to expose gaps early.

example-mapping.definition: A short structured workshop using coloured cards to break a story into rules, examples, and questions.

gherkin.definition: A structured Given-When-Then language for writing executable specifications readable by non-programmers.

living-documentation.definition: Documentation generated from the same executable specifications that verify the system, staying current by construction.

executable-specification.definition: A requirement captured precisely enough to be run as an automated test.

test-oracle.definition: The mechanism, human or automated, that decides whether an observed result is correct.

property-based-testing.definition: Asserting general invariants over thousands of generated inputs rather than handwritten examples.

shrinking.definition: Automatically minimising a failing generated input to the smallest case that still fails.

metamorphic-testing.definition: Checking relations between outputs of related inputs when a direct oracle is unavailable.

differential-testing.definition: Running identical inputs through multiple implementations and flagging output divergences.

back-to-back-testing.definition: Comparing a new implementation's outputs against a validated reference implementation.

model-based-testing.definition: Generating test cases automatically from a formal or behavioural model of the system.

combinatorial-testing.definition: Systematically covering interactions between parameters instead of exhaustive combinations.

pairwise-testing.definition: Ensuring every pair of parameter values appears in at least one test case.

orthogonal-array-testing.definition: Using statistical orthogonal arrays to cover multi-factor interactions with few runs.

classification-tree-method.definition: Partitioning the input space as a tree of aspects and classes, then combining classes into cases.

decision-table-testing.definition: Enumerating condition combinations and required actions as a truth-grid of business rules.

state-transition-testing.definition: Exercising valid and invalid transitions of a finite-state machine model.

cause-effect-graphing.definition: Deriving test cases from logical relationships between inputs (causes) and outputs (effects).

use-case-testing.definition: Designing tests from actor-goal use cases including main, alternate, and exception flows.

session-based-test-management.definition: Structuring exploratory testing into chartered, time-boxed, debriefed sessions with metrics.

test-charter.definition: A short mission statement scoping an exploratory session: what to explore and why.

heuristic-test-strategy-model.definition: A framework of product elements and quality criteria that guides test idea generation.

sfdipot.definition: Bach's product-elements heuristic: Structure, Function, Data, Interfaces, Platform, Operations, Time.

hiccupps.definition: Consistency-oracle heuristic: History, Image, Claims, Comparable products, User expectations, Product, Purpose, Standards.

oracle-problem.definition: The difficulty of determining the correct expected result for a given test input.

characterization-testing.definition: Pinning down existing behaviour of legacy code as a safety net before refactoring.

golden-master-testing.definition: Capturing approved reference outputs and flagging any deviation from them.

snapshot-testing.definition: Serialising rendered output or structures and comparing to a stored approved snapshot.

test-doubles.definition: Stand-ins for real dependencies: mocks, stubs, spies, and fakes.

consumer-driven-contract-testing.definition: Consumers publish expectations; providers verify they still honour every consumer's contract.

service-virtualization.definition: Simulating unavailable or costly dependencies to test integrations deterministically.

test-harness.definition: Automation scaffolding that executes tests, injects inputs, and captures results.

test-bed.definition: The configured environment and data set on which a test executes.

flaky-tests.definition: Tests that pass and fail non-deterministically, eroding trust in the suite.

test-quarantine.definition: Isolating flaky or failing tests from the main signal while they are triaged.

test-smell.definition: A structural symptom in test code indicating maintenance or reliability problems.

pesticide-paradox.definition: Repeatedly running the same tests stops finding new bugs; suites must evolve.

defect-clustering.definition: The empirical concentration of defects in a small number of modules or components.

fault-model.definition: The assumed set of faults a testing or verification technique is designed to detect.

fault-error-failure-chain.definition: The causal chain: a fault (defect) causes an error (bad state) that may cause a failure (observable deviation).

happy-path.definition: The default scenario where everything proceeds as expected without exceptions.

edge-case.definition: A scenario at the extreme boundary of operating parameters.

corner-case.definition: A scenario where multiple edge conditions coincide, often revealing compound defects.

negative-testing.definition: Deliberately supplying invalid inputs to confirm graceful and correct rejection.

sad-path-testing.definition: Exercising error, failure, and recovery flows rather than the successful path.

formal-verification.definition: Proving or disproving correctness of a system against a mathematical specification.

model-checking.definition: Exhaustively exploring a system's state space to verify temporal properties.

bounded-model-checking.definition: Searching for counterexamples within a bounded depth, trading totality for tractability.

temporal-logic-ltl-ctl.definition: Logics for expressing properties over time, such as safety and liveness, in model checking.

sat-solving.definition: Deciding propositional satisfiability; the engine behind many verification tools.

smt-solving.definition: Satisfiability modulo theories: SAT extended with arithmetic, arrays, bit-vectors, and more.

abstract-interpretation.definition: Soundly approximating program semantics over abstract domains to prove properties statically.

deductive-verification.definition: Proving program correctness by generating and discharging logical proof obligations.

hoare-logic.definition: Reasoning about programs with preconditions, postconditions, and invariants.

separation-logic.definition: An extension of Hoare logic for reasoning about heap-manipulating programs and aliasing.

design-by-contract.definition: Specifying preconditions, postconditions, and invariants as enforceable interface contracts.

loop-invariant.definition: A property that holds before and after every iteration, used to prove loops correct.

weakest-precondition.definition: The least restrictive precondition guaranteeing a postcondition after a statement executes.

refinement-types.definition: Types enriched with logical predicates, checked by SMT solvers at compile time.

dependent-types.definition: Types that depend on values, allowing specifications to be enforced in the type system itself.

typestate-analysis.definition: Tracking an object's protocol state through the type system to prevent illegal operation sequences.

formal-specification.definition: A precise, unambiguous mathematical description of required system behaviour.

refinement-mapping.definition: Relating an abstract specification to a concrete implementation to transfer proven properties.

interactive-theorem-proving.definition: Machine-checked proofs built with human guidance in tools like Coq, Isabelle, and Lean.

proof-carrying-code.definition: Code shipped with a machine-checkable proof of its safety properties.

runtime-verification.definition: Monitoring executing systems against formal properties and reacting to violations.

assertion-checking.definition: Embedding executable invariants in code to detect violated assumptions at runtime.

tla.definition: Lamport's specification language for modelling and model-checking concurrent and distributed algorithms.

alloy.definition: A lightweight relational modelling language with a bounded model finder and visualiser.

dafny.definition: A verification-aware language where the compiler proves pre/postconditions and invariants.

verus.definition: A Rust verifier using SMT and linear types to prove functional correctness of systems code.

frama-c.definition: An extensible analysis platform for C, combining abstract interpretation and deductive verification.

compcert.definition: A formally verified C compiler proven to preserve program semantics.

sel4.definition: A microkernel with machine-checked proofs of functional correctness and security enforcement.

kani.definition: A bounded model checker that verifies Rust programs against assertions and undefined behaviour.

miri.definition: An interpreter that detects undefined behaviour in Rust code, including aliasing violations.

mc-dc.definition: Modified Condition/Decision Coverage: each condition must independently affect the decision outcome.

structural-coverage-analysis.definition: Measuring which code structures tests exercised, required at high safety integrity levels.

conformance-test-suite.definition: A standardised battery of tests proving an implementation obeys a specification.

static-analysis.definition: Automated reasoning over code without execution to find defects, smells, and violations.

data-flow-analysis.definition: Tracking how values propagate through a program to reason about definitions and uses.

control-flow-graph.definition: A graph of basic blocks and branches representing all possible execution paths.

taint-analysis.definition: Tracking untrusted inputs through a program to detect injection-style vulnerabilities.

information-flow-analysis.definition: Proving that secret data cannot leak to public outputs, i.e., noninterference.

program-slicing.definition: Extracting the minimal statements that affect a chosen variable or point of interest.

symbolic-execution.definition: Executing a program with symbolic inputs, solving path constraints to generate tests or find bugs.

concolic-testing.definition: Combining concrete and symbolic execution to systematically explore paths and generate inputs.

coverage-guided-fuzzing.definition: A fuzzer mutating inputs while using code-coverage feedback to reach new paths.

structure-aware-fuzzing.definition: Fuzzing that mutates inputs respecting a grammar or format, such as protocols and file types.

grammar-based-fuzzing.definition: Generating inputs from a formal grammar to produce syntactically valid, deep-reaching cases.

differential-fuzzing.definition: Fuzzing two or more implementations in parallel and flagging behavioural divergence.

corpus-minimisation.definition: Reducing a fuzzing corpus to a smaller set that preserves the same code coverage.

oss-fuzz.definition: Google's continuous fuzzing service for critical open-source projects.

crash-triaging.definition: Deduplicating, classifying, and prioritising crashes produced by automated testing.

fault-localisation.definition: Automatically ranking the code locations most likely responsible for observed failures.

spectrum-based-fault-localisation.definition: Using pass/fail spectra of executed statements to rank suspicious code.

statistical-debugging.definition: Correlating runtime behaviour across runs to localise the cause of failures.

delta-debugging.definition: Automatically minimising a failing input or change set to the smallest reproduction.

automated-program-repair.definition: Generating candidate patches that make failing tests pass, filtered by heuristics.

sanitisers-asan-ubsan-tsan.definition: Compiler instrumentation detecting memory, undefined-behaviour, and threading errors at runtime.

data-race-detection.definition: Detecting unsynchronised concurrent accesses that produce undefined behaviour.

deadlock-detection.definition: Finding circular lock or resource dependencies that can halt progress permanently.

livelock.definition: A state where threads keep acting but make no progress, distinct from deadlock.

priority-inversion.definition: A high-priority task blocked by a low-priority one holding a shared resource.

git-bisection.definition: Binary-searching commit history to pinpoint the change that introduced a defect.

heisenbug.definition: A defect that changes or disappears when observed, often timing- or optimisation-sensitive.

core-dump-analysis.definition: Post-mortem inspection of a crashed process's memory image to diagnose faults.

record-and-replay-debugging.definition: Recording execution deterministically so a failure can be replayed and stepped through.

time-travel-debugging.definition: Reversing or replaying execution history to inspect earlier program states.

dynamic-binary-instrumentation.definition: Injecting analysis code into running binaries to trace and profile them without recompilation.

symbolication.definition: Translating raw addresses in stack traces into function names and source lines.

cyclomatic-complexity.definition: McCabe's count of linearly independent paths through code, a proxy for testability and risk.

cognitive-complexity.definition: A readability-focused measure of how hard control flow is for humans to follow.

npath-complexity.definition: The number of acyclic execution paths through a method; grows exponentially with branching.

halstead-metrics.definition: Software-science measures based on counts of distinct and total operators and operands.

lack-of-cohesion-of-methods-lcom.definition: A metric quantifying how weakly a class's methods share its fields.

fan-in-fan-out.definition: Counts of dependencies entering and leaving a module; coupling indicators.

connascence.definition: A precise taxonomy of coupling describing what must change together, and how strongly.

code-smell.definition: A surface symptom in code suggesting deeper design or maintainability problems.

technical-debt.definition: The implied future cost of shortcuts taken now in exchange for speed today.

technical-debt-quadrant.definition: Fowler's classification of debt as reckless/prudent and deliberate/inadvertent.

sqale-method.definition: A method for assessing code quality and estimating technical debt remediation cost.

maintainability-index.definition: A composite score from complexity, volume, and size predicting maintenance effort.

code-churn.definition: The amount of code added, modified, or deleted within a period, a strong defect predictor.

hotspot-analysis.definition: Combining complexity with change frequency to find the riskiest parts of a codebase.

defect-density.definition: Defects per unit of size, such as per thousand lines of code or per story point.

defect-removal-efficiency-dre.definition: The percentage of defects found before release versus those escaping.

defect-escape-rate.definition: The share of defects reaching production; a key quality-outcome measure.

orthogonal-defect-classification-odc.definition: IBM's scheme classifying defects by type and trigger to diagnose process weaknesses.

pareto-analysis-80-20.definition: Focusing on the small proportion of causes producing most defects or incidents.

software-reliability-growth-modelling.definition: Statistical models predicting failure rates and remaining defects from test data.

mutation-score.definition: The fraction of seeded faults detected by the test suite; a measure of suite strength.

equivalent-mutant.definition: A seeded fault that is behaviourally identical to the original, inflating mutation-score noise.

coverage-debt.definition: The backlog of untested or under-tested code that accumulates over time.

change-failure-rate.definition: The proportion of deployments that cause degraded service; one of the DORA four keys.

requirements-coverage.definition: The proportion of requirements exercised by at least one verified test.

iso-iec-25010.definition: The international product-quality model defining characteristics like reliability, security, and maintainability.

furps.definition: A quality-attribute taxonomy: Functionality, Usability, Reliability, Performance, Supportability, plus constraints.

quality-attribute-scenario.definition: A structured stimulus-response scenario used to make non-functional requirements testable.

service-level-indicator-sli.definition: A carefully defined quantitative measure of service health, such as success rate or latency.

service-level-objective-slo.definition: A target value or range for an SLI over a window, such as 99.9% success over 30 days.

service-level-agreement-sla.definition: A contractual commitment with consequences, typically looser than the internal SLO.

error-budget.definition: The tolerated amount of unreliability implied by an SLO, spent by incidents and releases.

error-budget-policy.definition: Pre-agreed actions that trigger when the error budget is exhausted, such as feature freezes.

burn-rate.definition: The speed at which an error budget is being consumed, relative to the pace that exhausts it exactly.

multi-window-multi-burn-rate-alerting.definition: SLO alerting that pairs short and long windows at several burn rates to balance precision and recall.

toil.definition: Manual, repetitive, automatable operational work that scales linearly with service growth.

on-call-rotation.definition: A scheduled rotation of engineers responsible for responding to production alerts.

escalation-policy.definition: Rules specifying whom to alert and when if an incident is unacknowledged or unresolved.

incident-command-system.definition: A defined command structure for major incidents with distinct command, ops, and communications roles.

incident-commander.definition: The single decision-maker coordinating response, communication, and priorities during an incident.

incident-severity-levels.definition: A classification scale tying impact to required response, escalation, and communication.

blameless-postmortem.definition: An incident review assuming good intent and focusing on systemic causes rather than individuals.

action-item-tracking.definition: Following postmortem remediation items to completion so lessons actually change systems.

five-whys.definition: Iteratively asking why to push past symptoms toward root causes.

ishikawa-fishbone-diagram.definition: A cause-and-effect diagram organising contributing factors into categories.

runbook.definition: Step-by-step operational procedures for handling known alerts, tasks, and failures.

playbook.definition: A broader operational guide covering classes of incidents, roles, and decision trees.

runbook-automation.definition: Encoding operational procedures as executable, auditable, and repeatable workflows.

auto-remediation.definition: Automatically correcting detected faults, with guardrails, before humans are paged.

self-healing-systems.definition: Systems that detect degradation and restore healthy state autonomously.

golden-signals.definition: Latency, traffic, errors, and saturation: the four signals for monitoring user-facing services.

red-method.definition: Per-service monitoring by Rate, Errors, and Duration.

use-method.definition: Per-resource monitoring of Utilisation, Saturation, and Errors.

availability-nines.definition: Expressing availability as 99%, 99.9%, 99.99% and the downtime each implies.

mean-time-to-detect-mttd.definition: Average time from fault onset to detection.

mean-time-to-acknowledge-mtta.definition: Average time from alert firing to a human acknowledging it.

mean-time-to-recover-mttr.definition: Average time to restore service after failure; also called failed-deployment recovery time in DORA.

mean-time-between-failures-mtbf.definition: Average operating time between consecutive failures of a repairable system.

recovery-time-objective-rto.definition: The maximum acceptable time to restore service after disruption.

recovery-point-objective-rpo.definition: The maximum acceptable data loss measured in time before disruption.

business-continuity-planning.definition: Preparing people, processes, and systems to keep critical functions running through disruption.

failover.definition: Automatically switching to a standby component, zone, or region upon failure.

failback.definition: Safely returning operations to the primary site after failover or maintenance.

active-active.definition: Running multiple replicas concurrently serving traffic for capacity and resilience.

active-passive.definition: Running a standby that takes over when the primary fails.

multi-region-deployment.definition: Running workloads in multiple geographic regions for latency, resilience, and compliance.

failure-domain.definition: An isolated unit whose failure does not affect other units, such as a rack, zone, or cell.

zone-redundancy.definition: Spreading instances across independent availability zones within a region.

load-shedding.definition: Deliberately rejecting or degrading low-priority work to protect critical paths under overload.

backpressure.definition: Signalling upstream producers to slow down when downstream capacity is exceeded.

retry-budget.definition: A cap on retry volume relative to successful requests to prevent retry-driven overload.

exponential-backoff-with-jitter.definition: Increasing retry delays exponentially and randomising them to avoid synchronised retry storms.

retry-storm.definition: Amplified traffic caused by clients aggressively retrying failing calls during an incident.

thundering-herd.definition: A synchronised surge of requests, often after a cache expiry or recovery, overwhelming a service.

request-coalescing.definition: Merging duplicate in-flight requests for the same resource into one upstream call.

hedged-requests.definition: Issuing duplicate requests to replicas and using the fastest response to cut tail latency.

tied-requests.definition: Hedged requests whose replicas cross-cancel once one begins execution, reducing wasted work.

graceful-degradation.definition: Continuing to serve a reduced but useful service when parts of the system fail.

graceful-shutdown.definition: Draining connections and completing in-flight work before terminating a process.

operational-readiness-review-orr.definition: A pre-launch review verifying monitoring, alerting, runbooks, and ownership are in place.

production-readiness-review-prr.definition: A structured gate assessing whether a service is safe and operable to run in production.

resilience-testing.definition: Validating that a system withstands injected faults and continues meeting its objectives.

denial-of-service-resilience.definition: Designing so that overload or attack degrades gracefully rather than collapsing entirely.

service-dependency-mapping.definition: Maintaining an accurate graph of runtime dependencies for impact analysis and incident response.

failure-mode-and-effects-analysis-fmea.definition: Systematically enumerating how each component can fail and the consequences of each failure mode.

safety-i.definition: A safety paradigm defined as the absence of adverse events, focused on what goes wrong.

safety-ii.definition: A safety paradigm defined as the ability to succeed under varying conditions, focused on what goes right.

resilience-potentials.definition: The four capabilities of resilient systems: responding, monitoring, anticipating, and learning.

etto-principle.definition: Hollnagel's Efficiency-Thoroughness Trade-Off: operators constantly trade rigour for speed.

fram-functional-resonance-analysis-metho.definition: Modelling complex systems as interacting functions whose variability can resonate into accidents.

functional-resonance.definition: Emergent system behaviour when normal performance variability across functions combines unexpectedly.

systemic-potentials-management-spm.definition: A structured method for assessing an organisation's four resilience potentials.

human-reliability-analysis-hra.definition: Quantifying and modelling the likelihood and mechanisms of human error in complex systems.

cream.definition: Hollnagel's Cognitive Reliability and Error Analysis Method for classifying human error contexts.

swiss-cheese-model.definition: Reason's model of accidents as aligned holes in successive layers of defence.

bow-tie-analysis.definition: Mapping threats, preventive barriers, the top event, mitigations, and consequences in one diagram.

barrier-analysis.definition: Examining which defences existed, how they failed, and which were missing after an incident.

normalization-of-deviance.definition: Gradual acceptance of out-of-spec practices as normal until disaster follows.

normal-accident-theory.definition: Perrow's thesis that tightly coupled, interactively complex systems inevitably produce accidents.

drift-into-failure.definition: Dekker's account of gradual organisational migration toward the boundary of safe operation.

stamp.definition: Leveson's Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes: accidents as failures of control, not of components.

stpa.definition: System-Theoretic Process Analysis: hazard analysis that identifies unsafe control actions in a control structure.

cast.definition: Causal Analysis based on STAMP: a blame-free accident analysis driven by control-structure flaws.

just-culture.definition: An accountability model distinguishing human error, at-risk behaviour, and recklessness in investigations.

safety-differently.definition: Dekker's movement reframing safety as the presence of capacity to succeed rather than absence of incidents.

high-reliability-organisation-hro.definition: Organisations achieving near-flawless operations in hazardous settings through preoccupation with failure and deference to expertise.

mindful-organising.definition: Weick's five practices enabling organisations to notice and contain unexpected events.

fmeda.definition: Failure Modes, Effects, and Diagnostic Analysis: FMEA extended with diagnostic coverage for functional safety.

fault-tree-analysis.definition: Deductive top-down analysis from an undesired event to combinations of contributing faults.

event-tree-analysis.definition: Inductive forward analysis of possible outcomes following an initiating event.

hazop.definition: Hazard and Operability study: systematic deviation analysis of a design's intentions using guide words.

stress-inoculation.definition: Deliberate practice under realistic pressure to build competence for high-stakes situations.

reliability-block-diagram.definition: A graphical model of how component reliabilities combine into system reliability.

common-cause-failure.definition: A single shared fault, such as a config or dependency, defeating multiple redundant components at once.

redundancy-n-1-2n.definition: Providing spare capacity or replicates so the loss of any single unit does not stop the service.

correlated-failure-analysis.definition: Finding hidden shared dependencies that make nominally independent replicas fail together.

survivorship-bias.definition: Drawing conclusions only from surviving systems or cases while ignoring the failures.

chaos-engineering.definition: Disciplined experimentation on a system to build confidence in its ability to withstand turbulent conditions.

steady-state-hypothesis.definition: A measurable definition of normal behaviour that a chaos experiment asserts must hold.

fault-injection.definition: Deliberately introducing faults such as latency, errors, or resource exhaustion to observe behaviour, and verifying error handling and recovery.

litmuschaos.definition: A CNCF chaos engineering framework providing a library of Kubernetes chaos experiments.

gremlin.definition: A commercial chaos engineering platform for controlled fault injection across infrastructure.

dirt-disaster-recovery-testing.definition: Netflix's programme of large-scale disaster and resilience exercises.

blast-radius-control.definition: Explicitly bounding the scope, targets, and abort conditions of a chaos experiment.

abort-conditions.definition: Predefined safety thresholds that immediately stop an experiment when exceeded.

network-emulation.definition: Simulating latency, loss, bandwidth limits, and partitions with tools such as tc/netem.

clock-skew-injection.definition: Shifting system time to expose assumptions about ordering, expiry, and synchronisation.

resource-exhaustion-testing.definition: Consuming CPU, memory, disk, or file descriptors to observe pressure behaviour.

game-day-facilitation.definition: Running structured failure rehearsals with defined objectives, roles, and learning capture.

fuzzing-for-resilience.definition: Randomised fault and input generation to surface unhandled states and crashes.

chaos-as-code.definition: Declaring chaos experiments in versioned configuration for repeatability and review.

three-pillars-of-observability.definition: Metrics, logs, and traces as complementary telemetry signal types.

distributed-tracing.definition: Following a request's path across services via linked spans to find latency and error sources.

span.definition: A single timed operation within a trace, with attributes, events, and parent-child relationships.

context-propagation.definition: Passing trace and correlation identifiers across process, service, and protocol boundaries.

w3c-trace-context.definition: The standard headers, traceparent and tracestate, for interoperable distributed tracing.

opentelemetry.definition: The vendor-neutral standard and SDK for generating, collecting, and exporting telemetry.

exemplar.definition: A sampled trace ID attached to a metric bucket, linking spikes directly to example traces.

cardinality.definition: The number of unique label combinations; high cardinality strains time-series systems and cost.

tail-based-sampling.definition: Deciding which traces to keep after they finish, preserving all errors and slow requests.

head-based-sampling.definition: Deciding trace sampling at request start, before outcomes are known.

continuous-profiling.definition: Always-on, low-overhead CPU and memory profiling of production workloads.

flame-graph.definition: A stacked visualisation of sampled stack frames showing where time is spent.

ebpf-observability.definition: Kernel-level tracing of syscalls, network, and applications without code changes.

real-user-monitoring-rum.definition: Capturing performance and errors from actual user sessions in the browser or app.

digital-experience-monitoring-dem.definition: End-to-end visibility into user experience across devices, networks, and applications.

application-performance-monitoring-apm.definition: Instrumentation and analytics for transaction traces, errors, and service dependencies.

structured-logging.definition: Emitting machine-parseable, key-value logs with consistent fields and correlation IDs.

log-aggregation.definition: Centralising logs from many sources with indexing, retention, and query capability.

alert-fatigue.definition: Desensitisation caused by excessive or noisy alerts, leading to missed real incidents.

alert-correlation.definition: Grouping related alerts into a single incident to reduce noise and speed diagnosis.

anomaly-detection.definition: Statistical or ML identification of unusual behaviour against baseline patterns.

aiops.definition: Applying ML and analytics to operational data for detection, correlation, and root-cause analysis.

root-cause-analysis.definition: Systematically determining the underlying cause of an incident or defect class.

topology-aware-rca.definition: Using a service dependency graph to trace a failure to its structural origin.

golden-dashboard.definition: A curated first-look dashboard showing the signals that matter most during incidents.

telemetry-pipeline.definition: The collection, processing, sampling, and routing path for observability data.

cardinality-explosion.definition: Unbounded label or dimension growth that degrades or bankrupts a metrics backend.

observability-driven-development.definition: Writing code with the telemetry it must emit as a first-class design concern.

ephemeral-environments.definition: Short-lived, per-branch environments enabling realistic testing and observability before merge.

queueing-theory.definition: The mathematics of waiting lines used to model and predict system latency and utilisation.

littles-law.definition: L = lambda x W: concurrency equals arrival rate times time in system, linking load and latency.

amdahls-law.definition: Speedup from parallelism is bounded by the serial fraction of the work.

universal-scalability-law-usl.definition: Gunther's throughput model adding contention and coherency penalties to Amdahl's law.

bottleneck-analysis.definition: Identifying the resource or dependency that limits overall throughput.

saturation.definition: The degree to which a resource has more work queued than it can serve.

percentile-latency-p50-p95-p99-p999.definition: Latency measured at tail percentiles, which averages hide and users actually feel.

tail-latency.definition: The slowest responses; at fan-out scale, they dominate real user experience.

coordinated-omission.definition: A measurement bias where closed-loop load generators stop sampling exactly during stalls.

open-vs-closed-loop-load.definition: Whether requests arrive independently at a fixed rate or only after the previous response.

throughput-vs-goodput.definition: Total work processed versus useful work completed within latency objectives.

service-time-vs-response-time.definition: Time to process a request versus time from arrival to completion including queueing.

queuing-delay.definition: Time a request waits before service begins; the hidden cost of utilisation near 100%.

utilisation-cliff.definition: The non-linear latency blow-up as resource utilisation approaches saturation.

capacity-planning.definition: Forecasting demand and provisioning resources to meet SLOs at acceptable cost.

performance-budget.definition: An explicit limit on latency, weight, or resource use that changes must not exceed.

benchmark-harness.definition: A controlled environment and methodology for reproducible performance measurement.

microbenchmarking.definition: Measuring isolated operations, with warm-up and statistical rigour, as in JMH.

warm-up-effects.definition: Early-run performance distortion from JIT compilation, caches, and pool filling.

jit-compilation.definition: Runtime compilation of hot code paths to native machine code for speed.

escape-analysis.definition: Compiler analysis moving heap allocations to the stack when they cannot escape.

garbage-collection-pauses.definition: Stop-the-world or concurrent GC phases that introduce latency spikes.

generational-gc.definition: Collecting young objects frequently and old objects rarely, exploiting object lifetimes.

heap-fragmentation.definition: Wasted memory from scattered free blocks degrading allocation and locality over time.

memory-leak-detection.definition: Finding allocations that are never released across long-running processes.

working-set.definition: The memory a process actively uses; exceeding physical RAM causes paging and stalls.

page-fault.definition: A CPU trap when a referenced page is absent from physical memory, incurring disk access.

cache-locality.definition: Arranging data access to reuse CPU cache lines and avoid memory stalls.

false-sharing.definition: Performance loss when independent variables share a cache line and invalidate each other.

cache-line.definition: The 64-byte unit of transfer between CPU caches and memory in modern processors.

numa-awareness.definition: Placing threads and memory on the same node to avoid cross-socket latency.

huge-pages.definition: Larger memory pages reducing TLB misses for memory-intensive workloads.

branch-prediction.definition: CPU speculation on control flow; mispredictions cost pipeline flushes.

simd-vectorisation.definition: Applying one instruction to many data lanes for throughput gains.

prefetching.definition: Anticipatory loading of data into caches before it is needed.

lock-contention.definition: Threads serialising on shared locks, negating parallelism.

lock-free-programming.definition: Algorithms using atomics and careful memory ordering instead of mutual exclusion.

wait-free-programming.definition: Strongest non-blocking guarantee: every thread completes in bounded steps.

memory-ordering-fences.definition: Rules and barriers governing visibility and ordering of memory operations across cores.

scalability-ceiling.definition: The load beyond which added resources reduce rather than raise throughput.

autoscaling-lag.definition: The delay between demand rising and new capacity becoming ready, causing transient overload.

right-sizing.definition: Matching resource allocation to actual measured demand to cut waste.

performance-regression-testing.definition: Continuous benchmarking in CI to catch latency and throughput regressions before release.

load-profile.definition: A defined mix, arrival pattern, and duration of traffic used in performance testing.

soak-duration.definition: Extended runtime in endurance tests long enough to expose slow leaks and drift.

latency-budget.definition: Allocating a total latency target across the components of a request path.

pareto-front-latency-vs-cost.definition: The set of configurations where no option improves latency without increasing cost.

cap-theorem.definition: Under a network partition, a distributed system must choose consistency or availability.

pacelc-theorem.definition: Extends CAP: even without partitions, systems trade latency against consistency.

acid-transactions.definition: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability guarantees for database transactions.

base.definition: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent: the alternative model to ACID.

linearizability.definition: The strongest consistency: operations appear instantaneous and respect real-time order.

sequential-consistency.definition: All processes observe operations in one global order consistent with each process's program order.

causal-consistency.definition: Causally related operations are seen in the same order everywhere; concurrent ones may differ.

eventual-consistency.definition: Replicas converge to the same state once updates stop, with no ordering guarantee meanwhile.

read-your-writes-consistency.definition: A client always sees its own prior writes.

monotonic-reads.definition: A client never observes data going backwards in time across reads.

snapshot-isolation.definition: Transactions read a consistent snapshot; write skew anomalies remain possible.

serializable-snapshot-isolation-ssi.definition: Snapshot isolation plus detection and abort of serialization conflicts.

strict-serializability.definition: Serializability plus real-time ordering, the strongest transactional guarantee.

quorum-r-w-n.definition: Tuning reads and writes so their quorums overlap, guaranteeing fresh reads.

sloppy-quorum.definition: Accepting writes on non-primary nodes to stay available, reconciled later.

hinted-handoff.definition: Temporarily storing writes for an unreachable replica and delivering them on recovery.

anti-entropy-repair.definition: Continuously comparing replicas and reconciling divergent data using Merkle trees.

merkle-tree.definition: A hash tree enabling efficient comparison of large data sets between replicas.

read-repair.definition: Fixing stale replicas opportunistically during reads.

vector-clock.definition: A per-node logical clock set capturing causal relationships and detecting conflicts.

lamport-timestamp.definition: A scalar logical clock establishing a partial order of events without physical time.

hybrid-logical-clock-hlc.definition: Combining physical time with logical counters for causally consistent, near-wall-clock timestamps.

crdt.definition: Conflict-free Replicated Data Types that merge deterministically without coordination.

last-writer-wins-lww.definition: A simple conflict-resolution rule using timestamps, at the cost of losing concurrent updates.

gossip-protocol.definition: Epidemic-style peer-to-peer dissemination of state for scalable membership and failure detection.

failure-detector.definition: A mechanism estimating whether a node is alive, with tunable suspicion and accuracy.

phi-accrual-failure-detector.definition: A probabilistic liveness detector emitting a suspicion level rather than a binary verdict.

consistent-hashing.definition: Hashing keys and nodes onto a ring so membership changes move minimal data.

virtual-nodes.definition: Multiple ring positions per physical node to smooth load distribution.

rendezvous-highest-random-weight-hashing.definition: Selecting the node with the highest hash of key and node ID, stable under membership change.

sharding.definition: Partitioning data across nodes to scale storage and throughput horizontally.

resharding.definition: Redistributing data across a changed number of shards with minimal disruption.

bloom-filter.definition: A compact probabilistic set membership test with false positives but no false negatives.

leader-election.definition: Choosing a single coordinator among nodes, safely, despite failures.

raft.definition: A consensus algorithm with leader election, log replication, and strong safety guarantees.

paxos.definition: The foundational consensus protocol family for agreeing on values in unreliable networks.

quorum-leases.definition: Time-bounded leadership grants preventing split-brain without per-request coordination.

fencing-token.definition: A monotonically increasing token rejecting stale leaders' writes to shared resources.

split-brain.definition: Two partitions each believing they are primary, producing divergent, conflicting writes.

byzantine-fault-tolerance.definition: Consensus that tolerates arbitrary or malicious faulty nodes, not just crashes.

flp-impossibility.definition: Deterministic consensus cannot be guaranteed to terminate in an asynchronous network with one faulty process.

two-generals-problem.definition: The impossibility of guaranteed agreement over an unreliable channel with bounded messages.

two-phase-commit-2pc.definition: An atomic commit protocol with a prepare phase and a commit phase, blocking on coordinator failure.

three-phase-commit-3pc.definition: A non-blocking-in-most-cases variant of 2PC adding a pre-commit phase and timeouts.

try-confirm-cancel-tcc.definition: Business-level distributed transactions reserving resources, then confirming or cancelling them idempotently.

saga-pattern.definition: Modelling a long transaction as local steps with compensating actions for rollback.

compensating-transaction.definition: A semantic undo of a completed step when a later step in a workflow fails.

transactional-outbox.definition: Writing events in the same database transaction as state changes, then relaying them reliably.

idempotent-consumer.definition: A consumer that safely processes duplicate deliveries by deduplicating on message identity.

exactly-once-semantics.definition: Processing guarantees where each message affects state exactly one time, usually via idempotence.

at-least-once-delivery.definition: Messages may be retried, so consumers must tolerate duplicates.

at-most-once-delivery.definition: Messages are never redelivered, but may be lost; fire-and-forget semantics.

poison-message.definition: A message that repeatedly fails processing and can block a queue without dead-lettering.

dead-letter-queue.definition: A holding queue for messages that exhausted retries, enabling inspection and replay.

split-brain-avoidance.definition: Design techniques, such as quorums and fencing, that prevent dual-primary divergence.

dual-write-problem.definition: The impossibility of atomically updating a database and an external system without a pattern like outbox.

distributed-lock.definition: A cluster-wide mutual exclusion primitive, typically lease- and fencing-based.

clock-synchronisation-ntp-ptp.definition: Keeping node clocks aligned; PTP reaches sub-microsecond precision for critical systems.

skew-tolerant-design.definition: Algorithms that stay correct despite unsynchronised or drifting clocks.

idempotency-key.definition: A client-supplied unique key letting servers safely collapse retried requests into one effect.

domain-driven-design-ddd.definition: Modelling software around the business domain, with a shared ubiquitous language and bounded contexts.

bounded-context.definition: An explicit boundary within which a domain model and its language are consistent.

ubiquitous-language.definition: One precise vocabulary shared by domain experts and developers inside a bounded context.

context-map.definition: A diagram of the relationships and integration patterns between bounded contexts.

anti-corruption-layer.definition: A translation layer insulating your model from a legacy or foreign model's concepts.

aggregate.definition: A consistency boundary of related entities with a single root enforcing invariants.

domain-event.definition: A recorded fact that something meaningful happened in the domain.

event-storming.definition: A collaborative workshop mapping domain events to discover boundaries and processes.

hexagonal-architecture-ports-and-adapter.definition: Isolating core logic behind ports with pluggable adapters for UI, storage, and transport.

clean-architecture.definition: Concentric layers with dependencies pointing inward, keeping business rules framework-free.

onion-architecture.definition: Domain model at the centre, with application and infrastructure layers depending inward.

layered-architecture.definition: Organising code into presentation, application, domain, and infrastructure layers.

modular-monolith.definition: A single deployable with strongly enforced internal module boundaries and contracts.

microservices.definition: Independently deployable services aligned to business capabilities and owned by small teams.

macroservices.definition: A middle ground: fewer, larger services than microservices but more modular than a monolith.

service-oriented-architecture-soa.definition: Enterprise-scale services with formal contracts and an integration backbone.

event-driven-architecture.definition: Components communicating by producing and consuming events asynchronously.

cqrs.definition: Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate write and read models optimised independently.

event-sourcing.definition: Persisting state as an append-only sequence of events, with state derived by replay.

projection.definition: A read model built by consuming and transforming an event stream.

strangler-fig-pattern.definition: Incrementally replacing a legacy system by routing slices of capability to new implementations.

big-bang-rewrite.definition: Replacing a system wholesale, a high-risk anti-pattern contrasted with incremental migration.

backend-for-frontend-bff.definition: Dedicated aggregation layer per client type, shaped to that client's needs.

api-gateway.definition: The single entry point handling routing, auth, throttling, and cross-cutting concerns.

service-mesh.definition: An infrastructure layer providing mTLS, retries, and telemetry for service-to-service traffic.

sidecar-proxy.definition: A co-deployed proxy intercepting a workload's traffic to add mesh capabilities.

ambient-mesh.definition: Sidecar-less service mesh using node-level and waypoint proxies to cut resource overhead.

control-plane-data-plane-separation.definition: Separating policy and configuration management from the path that carries live traffic.

operator-pattern.definition: Encoding operational knowledge in a controller that reconciles custom resources toward desired state.

reconciliation-loop.definition: Continuously comparing observed state with desired state and acting to close the gap.

declarative-configuration.definition: Specifying desired end state rather than imperative steps, letting systems converge to it.

immutable-infrastructure.definition: Replacing servers and images rather than mutating them in place.

infrastructure-as-code-iac.definition: Managing infrastructure through versioned, reviewed, machine-applied definitions.

gitops.definition: Git as the single source of truth, with agents continuously reconciling clusters to it.

configuration-drift.definition: Divergence between declared and actual state, detected and corrected by reconciliation.

serverless.definition: Running code without managing servers, billed by invocation or usage.

function-as-a-service-faas.definition: Event-triggered functions with managed scaling and per-invocation billing.

edge-computing.definition: Placing compute and data close to users or devices to cut latency and bandwidth.

microfrontends.definition: Independently developed and deployed frontend slices composed into one user experience.

twelve-factor-app.definition: Twelve principles for portable, scalable, operationally sound service applications.

cell-based-architecture.definition: Grouping all dependencies of a workload into isolated cells to contain failures to a fraction of users.

bulkhead-pattern.definition: Partitioning resources so exhaustion in one area cannot sink the whole system.

shuffle-sharding.definition: Giving each tenant a near-unique combination of resources so faults rarely align between them.

sidecar-pattern.definition: Attaching a helper process to a workload for logging, proxying, or syncing.

ambassador-pattern.definition: A proxy sidecar handling outbound connectivity concerns for an application.

adapter-pattern.definition: Translating one interface into another expected by a client.

circuit-breaker-state-machine.definition: Closed, open, and half-open states governing when calls to a failing dependency resume.

choreography-vs-orchestration.definition: Coordinating workflows by emergent event reactions versus a central conductor.

process-manager.definition: A stateful coordinator tracking a long-running distributed workflow's progress.

solid-principles.definition: Five object-oriented design principles: single responsibility, open-closed, Liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion.

dependency-inversion-principle.definition: High-level policy and low-level detail both depend on abstractions.

law-of-demeter.definition: An object should talk only to its immediate collaborators, limiting coupling.

dry-dont-repeat-yourself.definition: Every piece of knowledge should have a single, authoritative representation.

kiss.definition: Design simplicity should be a deliberate goal; complexity must earn its place.

yagni.definition: Do not build capability you do not yet need.

composition-over-inheritance.definition: Achieving reuse by combining behaviours rather than deep type hierarchies.

conways-law.definition: System designs mirror the communication structures of the organisations that build them.

inverse-conway-manoeuvre.definition: Restructuring teams deliberately to produce the architecture you want.

fitness-function-architecture.definition: An automated test that objectively guards an architectural characteristic.

architecture-decision-record-adr.definition: A short, dated document capturing a decision, its context, and consequences.

atam.definition: Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method: structured evaluation of architecture against quality attribute scenarios.

c4-model.definition: Four-level diagrams (context, container, component, code) for communicating software architecture.

quality-attribute-workshop.definition: Stakeholder session eliciting and prioritising quality attribute scenarios early.

seam.definition: A place in code where behaviour can be substituted without editing, enabling testing and migration.

object-relational-impedance-mismatch.definition: The structural friction between object models and relational schemas.

repository-pattern.definition: An abstraction mediating domain and data-mapping layers.

unit-of-work.definition: Tracking changes across a business transaction and committing them atomically.

specification-pattern.definition: Encapsulating business rules as composable, reusable predicate objects.

circuit-of-autonomy.definition: Keeping a cell's data plane functional without its control plane during outages.

rest.definition: Resource-oriented HTTP API style using standard methods, status codes, and representations.

graphql.definition: A typed query language letting clients request exactly the fields they need from one endpoint.

graphql-federation.definition: Composing multiple GraphQL services into a single unified supergraph.

grpc.definition: A high-performance RPC framework using HTTP/2, Protocol Buffers, streaming, and code generation.

protocol-buffers.definition: A compact, schema-driven binary serialisation format with strong evolution rules.

openapi-specification.definition: A machine-readable description of HTTP APIs, powering docs, SDKs, and contract tests.

asyncapi.definition: The equivalent of OpenAPI for event-driven and message-based interfaces.

json-schema.definition: A vocabulary for validating and documenting the structure of JSON documents.

cloudevents.definition: A CNCF specification standardising the envelope and metadata of event payloads.

webhooks.definition: Server-initiated HTTP callbacks pushing events to subscriber endpoints.

websocket.definition: A persistent, full-duplex protocol for low-latency bidirectional communication.

server-sent-events-sse.definition: A simple unidirectional server-to-client streaming channel over HTTP.

webrtc.definition: Real-time peer-to-peer audio, video, and data channels with NAT traversal.

mqtt.definition: A lightweight publish-subscribe protocol for constrained devices and unreliable networks.

amqp.definition: A message-oriented middleware standard with exchanges, queues, and routing semantics.

event-streaming.definition: Durable, ordered, replayable log-based messaging, as with Apache Kafka.

topic-and-partition.definition: Kafka's unit of stream naming and its ordered, scalable sub-division.

consumer-group.definition: Coordinated consumers sharing partitions of a topic for parallel, ordered processing.

log-compaction.definition: Retaining only the latest record per key in a stream to represent current state.

publish-subscribe.definition: Decoupled messaging where producers publish to topics and subscribers receive selectively.

point-to-point-messaging.definition: Queue semantics where each message is consumed by exactly one receiver.

message-broker.definition: Middleware providing routing, persistence, delivery, and flow control for messages.

schema-registry.definition: A central store enforcing compatibility of evolving message schemas.

schema-evolution.definition: Changing data schemas without breaking existing producers and consumers.

backward-forward-compatibility.definition: New readers can read old data, and old readers can read new data, respectively.

api-versioning.definition: Managing breaking interface change through versions in the path, header, or media type.

idempotent-rest-endpoints.definition: Endpoints designed so repeated identical requests yield the same effect.

optimistic-concurrency-etag-if-match.definition: Detecting conflicting concurrent updates using version tags rather than locks.

cursor-based-pagination.definition: Paging with stable opaque cursors instead of offsets that shift under writes.

token-bucket.definition: A rate-limiting algorithm allowing bursts up to a bucket size while enforcing average rate.

leaky-bucket.definition: A rate-limiting algorithm smoothing traffic to a constant outflow rate.

sliding-window-rate-limiting.definition: Rate limiting over a moving time window for smoother, fairer enforcement.

gcra-generic-cell-rate-algorithm.definition: A precise virtual-scheduling rate-limit algorithm used in modern API gateways.

delivery-semantics.definition: The at-most-once, at-least-once, or exactly-once guarantee a messaging path provides.

message-ordering-guarantees.definition: Promises about the relative order in which messages are delivered or processed.

backpressure-aware-streaming.definition: Streaming protocols that let consumers signal capacity to slow producers.

bulkhead-isolation-for-integrations.definition: Separating connection pools and quotas per dependency so one slow partner cannot starve others.

api-composition.definition: Aggregating responses from multiple services to satisfy a single client request.

aggregator-pattern.definition: A component that fans out calls and composes a unified response.

scatter-gather.definition: Broadcasting a request to many providers and combining the results.

content-negotiation.definition: Selecting representation format and language based on client preferences.

hypermedia-hateoas.definition: Responses including links that guide clients through available state transitions.

mtls-service-authentication.definition: Mutual certificate validation proving both client and server identity.

api-deprecation-policy.definition: A published contract for sunsetting API versions with migration windows.

http-2-multiplexing.definition: Many concurrent streams over one TCP connection, reducing head-of-line blocking.

http-3-over-quic.definition: HTTP over a UDP-based transport eliminating TCP head-of-line blocking and speeding handshakes.

long-polling.definition: Emulating push by holding requests open until data or timeout.

eventual-delivery.definition: Delivery guarantees under partition, with reconciliation and replay on recovery.

service-discovery.definition: Locating healthy service instances dynamically through registries or DNS-based mechanisms.

health-check-endpoints.definition: Liveness and readiness probes letting platforms route traffic and restart unhealthy instances.

etl-vs-elt.definition: Transforming data before versus after loading it into the target store.

medallion-architecture.definition: Layering data into bronze (raw), silver (cleansed), and gold (business-ready) zones.

lakehouse.definition: Combining data-lake economics with warehouse reliability via open table formats and ACID.

data-mesh.definition: Distributing data ownership to domains with data as a product, self-serve platform, and federated governance.

data-fabric.definition: A metadata-driven integration layer connecting distributed data sources with unified access.

data-contract.definition: An enforceable agreement on schema, semantics, quality, and SLAs between data producers and consumers.

data-product.definition: A discoverable, trustworthy, owned dataset or stream with defined interfaces and SLOs.

data-observability.definition: Monitoring freshness, volume, schema, distribution, and lineage to detect data incidents.

data-lineage.definition: Tracking the origin and transformations of data end to end for trust, debugging, and compliance.

columnar-storage.definition: Storing data by column for compression and fast analytical scans.

parquet-orc.definition: Columnar file formats with encoding, statistics, and predicate pushdown for analytics.

predicate-pushdown.definition: Pushing filters into storage or scans to read less data.

partition-pruning.definition: Skipping irrelevant partitions using metadata to cut scan cost.

vectorised-execution.definition: Processing data in batches through CPU-friendly columnar operators for speed.

mpp-massively-parallel-processing.definition: Distributing query work across many nodes with parallel scans, joins, and exchanges.

dimensional-modelling.definition: Structuring analytics around facts and dimensions for understandable, fast queries.

star-snowflake-schema.definition: Fact tables joined directly to denormalised dimensions, or to normalised dimension hierarchies.

slowly-changing-dimensions-scd.definition: Patterns for tracking attribute history over time (Types 1, 2, 3).

data-vault.definition: A modelling approach with hubs, links, and satellites designed for auditability and change.

change-data-capture-cdc.definition: Streaming row-level database changes from transaction logs to downstream systems.

lambda-architecture.definition: Parallel batch and speed layers reconciled by a serving layer for accurate, low-latency views.

kappa-architecture.definition: A single streaming pipeline for both real-time and reprocessing, eliminating the batch layer.

event-time-vs-processing-time.definition: Distinguishing when events occurred from when they are handled by the pipeline.

watermarking-streams.definition: Tracking event-time progress to decide when windowed results are complete.

windowing-tumbling-sliding-session.definition: Grouping unbounded streams into finite aggregation windows of different shapes.

late-arriving-data-handling.definition: Policies for events that appear after their window has closed, such as allowed lateness and side outputs.

exactly-once-stream-processing.definition: Checkpointed, transactional stream state giving end-to-end single-effect semantics.

stateful-stream-processing.definition: Maintaining and checkpointing operator state such as joins, aggregates, and session buffers.

data-skew.definition: Uneven partition sizes causing stragglers and wasted cluster capacity.

salting-skew-handling.definition: Adding synthetic key variance to spread hot keys across partitions.

shuffle.definition: Redistributing data across nodes for joins and aggregations, often the dominant cost.

broadcast-join.definition: Replicating a small table to every node to avoid a costly shuffle.

small-files-problem.definition: Excessive tiny files degrading query planning and object-store throughput.

compaction.definition: Merging small files or log segments to restore efficient storage layout.

time-travel-tables.definition: Querying a table as of a past snapshot or version for reproducibility and audit.

open-table-format.definition: Table standards like Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Hudi adding ACID, evolution, and snapshots to object storage.

data-catalog.definition: An inventory of datasets with schema, ownership, lineage, and search metadata.

active-metadata.definition: Metadata that drives automation, recommendations, and governance actions, not just documentation.

master-data-management.definition: Creating trusted golden records for core entities across systems.

golden-record.definition: The single reconciled, authoritative representation of a business entity.

entity-resolution.definition: Determining when records from different sources refer to the same real-world entity.

fuzzy-matching.definition: Approximate string and record matching using edit distance, phonetics, or embeddings.

data-quality-dimensions.definition: Accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, and uniqueness as measurable axes.

data-freshness-sla.definition: A commitment on maximum staleness of a dataset or stream.

backfill.definition: Reprocessing historical data after logic, schema, or bug fixes.

idempotent-ingestion.definition: Loading pipelines that can safely re-run without duplicating data.

upsert-merge.definition: Atomically inserting or updating rows based on key match conditions.

orchestration-dag.definition: A directed acyclic graph of tasks with dependencies, retries, and SLAs.

reverse-etl.definition: Pushing warehouse-modelled data back into operational tools like CRMs.

data-lake-governance.definition: Access control, cataloguing, lineage, and retention policies across a data lake.

pii-discovery.definition: Automatically locating personal data across stores for protection and compliance.

anonymisation-vs-pseudonymisation.definition: Irreversibly removing identifiability versus replacing identifiers with reversible tokens.

metric-layer-semantic-layer.definition: Centralising metric definitions so every consumer computes the same number.

analytics-engineering.definition: Applying software engineering practices to SQL-based data transformation and modelling.

data-downtime.definition: Periods when data is missing, stale, or wrong, and its business cost.

data-sla-monitoring.definition: Alerting on freshness, volume, and quality breaches in pipelines.

data-reliability-engineering.definition: Applying SRE disciplines, SLOs, and incident response to data platforms.

write-ahead-log-wal.definition: Durably recording changes before applying them, enabling crash recovery.

mvcc.definition: Multi-Version Concurrency Control letting readers and writers proceed without blocking.

snapshot-reads.definition: Reading a consistent point-in-time view while writes continue.

b-tree-index.definition: A balanced, high-fanout tree index making range and point queries efficient.

lsm-tree.definition: A write-optimised storage engine using memtables, sorted runs, and compaction.

write-amplification.definition: Bytes written to storage per logical byte written, a key SSD-endurance and throughput cost.

read-amplification.definition: Disk reads required per logical read, reduced by bloom filters and caches.

space-amplification.definition: Storage overhead relative to live data, driven by versions and compaction lag.

compaction-strategy.definition: Scheduling and algorithms for merging LSM levels, trading write, read, and space cost.

memtable.definition: The in-memory write buffer of an LSM store, flushed to sorted immutable files.

sstable.definition: An immutable, sorted, on-disk key-value file underlying LSM engines.

tombstone.definition: A deletion marker in append-only and distributed stores, purged after safe expiry.

buffer-pool.definition: The cache of disk pages in memory, with eviction policies and dirty-page flushing.

query-planner.definition: The component translating SQL into a physical execution plan of operators.

cost-based-optimisation.definition: Choosing plans by estimated cost using statistics and cardinality estimates.

cardinality-estimation.definition: Predicting intermediate result sizes; estimation errors are the dominant cause of bad plans.

statistics-and-histograms.definition: Summaries of column distributions that feed selectivity and cost estimation.

selectivity.definition: The fraction of rows a predicate matches, central to join ordering and plan choice.

join-algorithms.definition: Nested loop, hash, merge, and index joins with different complexity and memory profiles.

index-only-scan.definition: Serving a query entirely from an index without touching the table.

covering-index.definition: An index containing all columns a query needs.

partial-index.definition: An index over only rows matching a predicate, reducing size and maintenance cost.

query-plan-regression.definition: A formerly fast query slowing because the planner chose a different plan.

connection-pooling.definition: Reusing database connections to avoid handshake and process overhead under load.

connection-pool-exhaustion.definition: All pooled connections busy, causing queueing, timeouts, and cascading failures.

deadlock-database.definition: Cyclic lock waits resolved by aborting one transaction.

lock-contention-database.definition: Transactions serialising on the same rows, pages, or tables.

advisory-lock.definition: An application-level lock primitive provided by the database without row coupling.

autovacuum-vacuum.definition: Reclaiming space from dead MVCC versions and refreshing planner statistics.

transaction-isolation-levels.definition: Read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, serializable: increasing anomaly protection.
