write-skew.definition: An anomaly where two transactions each read overlapping data and write disjoint rows, breaking invariants.

phantom-read.definition: A transaction seeing new rows matching its predicate that appeared since it began.

htap.definition: Hybrid transactional/analytical processing serving both workloads from one system.

oltp.definition: Online transaction processing: many short, concurrent, row-oriented read/write transactions.

olap.definition: Online analytical processing: large scans, aggregations, and columnar workloads.

materialised-view.definition: A precomputed query result persisted and refreshed for fast reads.

incremental-view-maintenance.definition: Updating materialised results from deltas instead of full recomputation.

change-streams.definition: Database-provided streams of committed changes for reactive and integration use.

keyset-pagination.definition: Paging with an indexed seek predicate rather than OFFSET scans.

hot-partition.definition: A single key or shard absorbing most traffic, negating scaling.

table-scan-vs-index-seek.definition: Reading all rows versus descending an index directly to matching keys.

vector-database.definition: A store indexing high-dimensional embeddings for similarity search.

approximate-nearest-neighbour-ann.definition: Trading exactness for speed when searching high-dimensional vector spaces.

hnsw.definition: Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs: a fast, high-recall vector index.

ivf-product-quantisation.definition: Inverted-file and compression techniques shrinking vector indexes for scale.

object-storage-consistency.definition: The read-after-write and list consistency guarantees of blob stores, and their limits.

storage-tiering.definition: Moving data across hot, warm, and cold tiers as access patterns change.

erasure-coding.definition: Storing data with redundancy math instead of full replicas, cutting storage overhead.

quorum-writes-and-reads.definition: Coordinating replica acknowledgements to guarantee consistent reads.

backup-vs-snapshot-vs-replication.definition: Three distinct protection mechanisms with different recovery and consistency properties.

point-in-time-recovery-pitr.definition: Restoring a database to an arbitrary moment using backups plus log replay.

gitflow.definition: A heavyweight branching model with develop, release, and hotfix branches.

feature-flags-toggles.definition: Runtime switches decoupling deployment from release and enabling instant rollback.

progressive-delivery.definition: Gradually exposing releases via canaries, flags, and rings with automated analysis.

canary-deployment.definition: Routing a small traffic slice to a new version, then expanding on success.

blue-green-deployment.definition: Two identical environments with traffic switched atomically between them.

rolling-deployment.definition: Replacing instances incrementally while keeping the service available.

ring-deployment.definition: Staged exposure through ordered cohorts such as internal, beta, and regional rings.

dark-launch.definition: Shipping code to production without exposing it to users, often to test load and behaviour.

automated-canary-analysis.definition: Statistically comparing canary and baseline metrics to gate promotion automatically.

merge-queue.definition: Batching and validating merges against the latest trunk to keep main always green.

stacked-diffs.definition: Small, dependent change series reviewed independently for faster, safer integration.

monorepo.definition: One repository holding many projects with shared tooling and atomic cross-project changes.

hermetic-build.definition: A build isolated from network and ambient state for reproducibility and supply-chain integrity.

artifact-registry.definition: A governed store for versioned build artifacts and container images.

semantic-versioning.definition: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH versioning signalling the compatibility impact of changes.

conventional-commits.definition: A commit message convention enabling automated changelogs and version bumps.

environment-promotion.definition: Advancing the same immutable artifact through dev, staging, and production.

configuration-as-code.definition: Version-controlling application and environment configuration with review and audit.

secretless-deployment.definition: Using workload identity and short-lived credentials instead of stored secrets.

progressive-rollout-automation.definition: Tooling such as Argo Rollouts and Flagger that shifts traffic and enforces analysis gates.

pipeline-as-code.definition: Defining CI/CD workflows in versioned files alongside the application.

test-parallelisation.definition: Splitting test suites across workers to cut feedback time.

shifting-security-left.definition: Embedding security checks into design, code, and pipelines rather than post-release gates.

release-engineering.definition: The discipline of building reliable, repeatable, auditable release processes and tooling.

internal-developer-platform-idp.definition: A self-service product layer over infrastructure enabling developers to ship independently.

self-service-provisioning.definition: Developers creating environments and resources on demand without tickets.

platform-as-a-product.definition: Running the internal platform with product management, user research, and adoption metrics.

progressive-context-propagation.definition: Distributed context that follows work across pipelines, deploys, and runtime for traceability.

gvisor-kata-firecracker.definition: Stronger isolation options: user-space kernels, lightweight VMs, and microVMs for untrusted workloads.

unikernel.definition: A single-address-space image bundling application with a minimal kernel library.

webassembly-wasm.definition: A portable, sandboxed bytecode format for near-native execution across environments.

wasi.definition: A system-interface standard giving Wasm modules controlled access to files, clocks, and sockets.

seccomp-capabilities-namespaces.definition: Layered Linux hardening primitives reducing what a compromised process can do.

secure-compilation.definition: Compiler techniques that preserve security properties and mitigate undefined behaviour.

undefined-behaviour.definition: Program states the language standard does not define, enabling aggressive, unsafe optimisations.

memory-safety.definition: Guarantees preventing out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, and related classes of bugs.

ownership-borrow-checking.definition: Compile-time enforcement of aliasing and lifetime rules to guarantee memory safety.

virtual-clock-and-monotonic-time.definition: Choosing monotonic versus wall-clock time sources to avoid clock-jump bugs.

graceful-restart-and-state-snapshotting.definition: Persisting state so processes can restart quickly without losing progress.

green-software-engineering.definition: Building software that consumes less energy and emits less carbon across its lifecycle.

software-carbon-intensity-sci.definition: The ISO/IEC 21031 rate metric: operational plus embodied emissions per functional unit.

embodied-carbon.definition: Emissions from manufacturing and disposing of the hardware a workload uses.

operational-carbon.definition: Emissions from the electricity consumed while software runs.

carbon-intensity-of-electricity.definition: Grams of CO2e per kilowatt-hour, varying by grid region and time of day.

carbon-aware-computing.definition: Shifting flexible workloads in time or region to lower-carbon energy.

energy-proportionality.definition: Designing systems whose power draw scales with utilisation rather than idling high.

power-usage-effectiveness-pue.definition: Total data-centre power divided by IT power, measuring overhead efficiency.

water-usage-effectiveness-wue.definition: Litres of water per kilowatt-hour of IT load, a data-centre sustainability metric.

idle-power-draw.definition: Energy consumed by servers doing little or no useful work.

software-efficiency.definition: Delivering the same functionality with fewer CPU cycles, memory, and I/O.

zombie-servers.definition: Provisioned resources with negligible utilisation that still consume power.

carbon-reporting-for-software.definition: Instrumenting and disclosing software emissions alongside cost and performance.

sustainable-by-default-architecture.definition: Choosing patterns and regions that minimise emissions without user intervention.

nisq.definition: The Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum era: limited qubits, high error rates, no full error correction.

quantum-error-correction-qec.definition: Encoding logical qubits across many physical qubits to detect and correct errors.

surface-code.definition: A leading topological QEC code on a 2D grid with local stabiliser measurements.

logical-vs-physical-qubit.definition: The error-corrected unit of computation versus the noisy hardware qubit beneath it.

decoherence.definition: Loss of quantum information to environmental interaction within a coherence time.

gate-fidelity.definition: The probability that a quantum operation implements its intended unitary correctly.

circuit-transpilation.definition: Rewriting a quantum circuit to match hardware topology and native gate sets.

qubit-topology-and-routing.definition: Limited physical connectivity forcing SWAP-based routing that adds noise and depth.

circuit-depth.definition: The number of sequential gate layers, constrained by coherence before errors dominate.

variational-quantum-eigensolver-vqe.definition: A hybrid classical-quantum algorithm for estimating ground-state energies.

qaoa.definition: The Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm: variational search over combinatorial problems.

hybrid-quantum-classical-loop.definition: Iterating a parameterised quantum circuit under classical optimisation.

error-mitigation-zne.definition: Extrapolating results to zero noise to improve estimates on noisy hardware.

quantum-advantage.definition: Demonstrated practical superiority of a quantum approach over the best classical alternative.

quantum-circuit-simulation.definition: Classically emulating quantum circuits for development and verification.

post-quantum-migration-planning.definition: Inventorying cryptography and sequencing replacement with quantum-resistant algorithms.

playtesting.definition: Observing real players to evaluate comprehension, fun, difficulty, and emotional response.

netcode.definition: The networking layer synchronising multiplayer game state across clients and servers.

tick-rate.definition: How often the authoritative server advances its simulation.

client-prediction-and-reconciliation.definition: Predicting locally and correcting when authoritative state arrives.

rollback-netcode.definition: Rewinding and re-simulating when predicted remote inputs prove wrong.

lag-compensation.definition: Rewinding world state to validate hits based on the shooter's perceived time.

server-authoritative-architecture.definition: Game logic run on servers so clients cannot cheat by editing state.

deterministic-simulation.definition: Bit-identical simulation results across machines enabling lockstep and replay.

frame-pacing.definition: Delivering frames at even intervals to avoid judder.

frame-time-percentiles.definition: Measuring frame-time stability via high percentiles and 1% lows, not just averages.

input-latency.definition: End-to-end delay from player action to on-screen response.

trc-tcr-certification.definition: Platform holder technical requirement compliance gates for console release.

soak-testing-online-games.definition: Extended multiplayer sessions to expose leaks, desync, and degradation.

live-ops.definition: Operating a game as a service with events, updates, telemetry, and balancing.

game-telemetry-and-balance-analytics.definition: Using player data to tune difficulty, economy, and matchmaking.

anti-cheat.definition: Detecting and preventing client tampering, aim assistance, and automation.

matchmaking-sbmm-eomm.definition: Pairing players by skill or engagement for fairness and retention.

xr-comfort-testing.definition: Validating motion, latency, and rendering choices that cause sim sickness.

motion-to-photon-latency.definition: The delay from head movement to updated display, critical in VR.

reprojection-timewarp.definition: Re-projecting frames using fresh tracking data to reduce perceived latency.

refactoring.definition: Improving internal structure without changing external behaviour.

spike-solution.definition: A time-boxed investigation to reduce uncertainty before committing to a design.

walking-skeleton.definition: A minimal end-to-end implementation touching every architectural layer.

prototype.definition: A throwaway or evolutionary build for learning, not production use.

big-ball-of-mud.definition: A system without discernible architecture, where expedient patches dominate.

broken-windows-theory-software.definition: Visible neglect invites further decay; keeping small problems fixed preserves quality culture.

boy-scout-rule.definition: Leave the codebase cleaner than you found it.

code-review.definition: Structured peer inspection of changes for correctness, clarity, and risk.

pair-programming.definition: Two developers at one workstation, continuously reviewing and designing together.

mob-programming.definition: The whole team collaborating on one change at one screen.

retrospective.definition: A recurring team reflection on what worked and what to change next.

kaizen.definition: Continuous, incremental improvement as a sustained practice.

poka-yoke-error-proofing.definition: Designing so mistakes are impossible or immediately visible.

technology-radar.definition: A periodic, opinionated map of technologies to adopt, trial, assess, or hold.

wardley-mapping.definition: Mapping value chains against evolution to inform strategic technology decisions.

architecture-kata.definition: A practice exercise for honing design judgement on realistic problems.

timeboxing.definition: Fixing a maximum duration for an activity to impose focus and limit scope.

error-budget-release-gating.definition: Blocking risky releases while reliability objectives are already breached.

engineering-ladder-and-competency-model.definition: Structured progression criteria aligning growth with expected impact.

build-vs-buy-vs-adopt.definition: Deciding between building capability, procuring it, or adopting open source, using total cost of ownership.

total-cost-of-ownership-tco.definition: The full lifecycle cost of a system including operation, migration, and exit.

cost-per-transaction.definition: Unit economics of a service, exposing scale inefficiencies and regression risk.

unit-economics-for-software.definition: Revenue or value per unit of compute or user, guiding architectural trade-offs.

finops.definition: Managing cloud spend as an engineering discipline with ownership and accountability.

focus-specification.definition: An open specification standardising cloud billing data for cost analysis.

cost-anomaly-detection.definition: Automatically flagging unexpected spend spikes and their causes.

showback-and-chargeback.definition: Attributing infrastructure cost to teams to drive efficient design.
